longForm.title: Battle of Dak To, 1967: Hill 875 and the PAVN's Operational Trap
longForm.excerpt: In November 1967, the PAVN's 1st Division drew US forces into a costly attritional battle on the ridgelines of Kontum Province. The fight for Hill 875 cost the 173rd Airborne Brigade 376 killed. Three months later, the Tet Offensive began.
paragraphs: Kontum Province in the Central Highlands of South Vietnam sits on a network of ridgelines running east-west toward the Cambodian border. The terrain is steep, triple-canopy jungle cut by streambeds and ridgelines that channel movement and make fire support coordination a persistent problem. In November 1967, the North Vietnamese Army's 1st Division — specifically the 32nd, 66th, and 174th Regiments — moved into the Dak To area with a clearly defined operational objective: draw US forces into costly ridge-line fighting on ground of the PAVN's choosing, inflict maximum casualties, and disengage before destruction. MACV intelligence had detected the buildup in the weeks prior. The 4th Infantry Division reinforced the Dak To Special Forces camp. None of that changed what happened next.

The PAVN plan at Dak To followed a pattern visible in earlier Central Highlands engagements: occupy fortified hilltop positions, force US units to attack uphill against prepared defenses, and create conditions where American fire support advantages were degraded by terrain, weather, and the proximity of their own troops. This was not a conventional defense of terrain. The PAVN was using terrain as an operational tool to control the terms of engagement and the rate of US attrition. When elements of the 4th Infantry Division made contact on 3 November, they were already inside a shaping operation that the PAVN had been preparing for weeks.

The engagements between 3 and 11 November were costly but not decisive. US units — including the 1st Battalion, 12th Infantry Regiment of the 4th Infantry Division — fought a series of actions on the ridgelines west and north of Dak To against the 32nd and 66th Regiments. The pattern was consistent: US forces advancing uphill under heavy fire from PAVN positions in prepared fighting holes, fire support requests complicated by weather and canopy, air strikes delivered against targets that the jungle concealed until contact was made. The 173rd Airborne Brigade was committed to reinforce on 12 November. General William Peers, commanding the 4th Infantry Division, had by then recognized that the PAVN intended a decisive engagement somewhere on the ridge system and was waiting to determine where.

Hill 875 is a ridgeline feature approximately 9 kilometers southwest of Dak To. By 17 November, intelligence indicated that the 174th Regiment of the 1st NVA Division had occupied it in strength. The 2nd Battalion, 503rd Infantry Regiment, 173rd Airborne Brigade — designated 2/503 — received orders to clear it. The battalion moved out on 19 November with two assault companies in column. The terrain was steep gradients and dense vegetation with limited visibility. What the maps did not show was the extent of PAVN preparation. The 174th Regiment had constructed a fortified complex of bunkers, spider holes, and interconnecting trenches, much of it covered by overhead logs and earth, that had survived pre-assault air and artillery bombardment with significant sections intact.

At approximately 1000 hours on 19 November, 2/503 made contact and immediately took heavy casualties. The lead companies were pinned down on the slope. The battalion attempted to consolidate but was engaged from multiple directions simultaneously. Then, at approximately 1158 hours, a US Air Force F-100 Super Sabre released two 500-pound bombs on the battalion command group and the wounded collection point. The error killed 42 soldiers and wounded 45 more, including the battalion executive officer. Whether the incident resulted from misidentification of target coordinates, unclear marking by the ground force, or a navigation error by the aircraft was never definitively established. The effect was not ambiguous: 2/503 was reduced to a defensive perimeter with no ability to advance or withdraw as darkness fell.

The 4th Battalion, 503rd Infantry arrived to reinforce on 20 November, but the terrain and PAVN position made rapid relief impossible. The relief force fought uphill through the same conditions that had stopped 2/503. The combined force resumed the assault on 22 November. By this point the PAVN 174th Regiment had begun to withdraw — the extended engagement had served its purpose — and the crest of Hill 875 was taken on 23 November, Thanksgiving Day 1967. The timing produced media coverage the Army's public affairs office had not anticipated and had no effective answer for.

The tactical lessons from Dak To, and from Hill 875 specifically, were not new but they were reinforced with considerable weight. The PAVN's decision to fight on carefully selected terrain and disengage before complete destruction was sound operational practice that US commanders found difficult to counter within any single engagement's time frame. Air and artillery support — the US force's primary force multipliers — were significantly degraded by terrain and weather throughout. The friendly fire incident on 19 November was an operational tragedy, but it also reflected a genuine coordination problem in close jungle terrain that the communications and navigation technology of 1967 could not reliably solve, regardless of training standards.

The 173rd Airborne Brigade suffered 376 killed and 1,441 wounded during the Dak To campaign. The 4th Infantry Division contributed substantial additional casualties. US military estimates put PAVN dead at approximately 1,644, though the methodology behind that figure cannot be independently verified. The engagement fulfilled the PAVN operational objective: it drew major US combat power into a costly attritional fight in terrain of the enemy's choosing, at a moment — late 1967 — when Hanoi was finalizing preparations for the Tet Offensive. Whether Dak To was conceived as a deliberate diversion for Tet, or whether the two operations were developed independently and the timing was coincidental, remains a genuine question in the operational histories of the war. The gap in the record has not been closed.

shortForm.title: Operation Starlite, 1965: The First US Offensive in Vietnam
shortForm.excerpt: On 18 August 1965, US Marines landed on the Van Tuong Peninsula in the first major US offensive operation in Vietnam. Operation Starlite destroyed a Viet Cong battalion. It also taught the enemy the cost of standing and fighting — a lesson the PAVN absorbed and acted on.
paragraphs: The Van Tuong Peninsula in Quang Ngai Province juts south into the South China Sea approximately 16 kilometers south of Chu Lai, where the 1st Marine Aircraft Wing had been operating since March 1965. In August, a defector reported that the 1st Viet Cong Regiment — specifically its 60th and 80th Battalions — was concentrated on the peninsula and preparing to attack the Chu Lai airfield. III Marine Amphibious Force had three days to plan and execute a response. The operation that launched on 18 August 1965 was the first regimental-sized offensive action conducted by US forces in the Vietnam War.

The plan combined amphibious assault from the sea with helicopter-borne insertion inland, designed to encircle the VC force before it could withdraw into the treeline and disperse. The 3rd Battalion, 7th Marines inserted by helicopter into a blocking position south and west of the peninsula. The 2nd Battalion, 4th Marines landed from amphibious ships on the eastern coast. Artillery and naval gunfire were pre-positioned to cut off avenues of escape. The coordination executed close to plan — which, for a force that had not conducted a combined arms encirclement against a prepared enemy in this theater, was not guaranteed. The blocking position held. The VC battalion attempted to break through it and could not.

The operation ran 18-24 August. US forces reported 614 VC killed and 9 captured against losses of 45 killed and 203 wounded. The casualty figures have been accepted by subsequent historians as broadly accurate, though the distinction between combatants and non-combatants in the body count was not always methodologically sound. What Operation Starlite demonstrated operationally was that combined arms encirclement could destroy a VC main force unit that lacked the mobility to break contact. The 1st VC Regiment took severe losses at Van Tuong. It also absorbed the operational lesson: standing and accepting a fixed engagement against US combined arms was not survivable. That lesson shaped the character of every subsequent major engagement in the war, and the PAVN adjusted its doctrine accordingly — which is why the battles that followed were so much harder to force on terms favorable to the Americans.

onThisDay.headline: Aircraft from USS Yorktown Strike Japanese Forces at Tulagi, Opening the Battle of the Coral Sea
onThisDay.summary: On 4 May 1942, aircraft from the USS Yorktown (CV-5) attacked Japanese naval forces that had occupied Tulagi in the Solomon Islands, opening the Battle of the Coral Sea. The five-day engagement that followed — concluding on 8 May — was the first naval battle in history in which opposing surface ships never came within sight of each other, fought entirely by carrier aircraft.
